## Motivation: Evaluating LLMs is hard!

```{=latex}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<1-> Human evaluation is the \textbf{gold standard}, but \textbf{slow} and \textbf{expensive}.
  \item<2-> The authors use state-of-the-art LLMs, like GPT-4, as a \textbf{surrogate} for humans.
\end{itemize}

\vspace{-0.4em}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.6\linewidth}
\begin{itemize}
  \item[]\vspace{-0.75em}\begin{itemize}
    \item<3-> Trained with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).
    \item<3-> Tend to better match humans. 
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.8em}
\visible<4->{%
\centering{\Large\bfseries\color{structure} $\rightarrow$ LLM-as-a-Judge}\par}
\vspace{0.5em}
\visible<5->{\centering\small Tried before, but never studied systematically.\par}
\end{minipage}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.38\linewidth}
\vspace{0pt}
\visible<4->{\centering\includegraphics[height=1.3in]{images/judge724_crop.png}\par}
\end{minipage}
```

## Example 1 - Follow-up:

```{=latex}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=gray!6, colframe=gray!45, boxrule=0.4pt, arc=2mm,
  left=5pt, right=5pt, top=3pt, bottom=4pt,
  title={\sffamily Follow-up Question}, fonttitle=\scriptsize\bfseries,
  coltitle=black, colbacktitle=gray!18]
\ttfamily\scriptsize\raggedright
How does it affect my daily life? Give 3 examples
\end{tcolorbox}
\vspace{-0.6em}
\onslide<2->{%
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.32\textwidth}
\begin{chatbox}[colback=blue!5, equal height group=followup, fontupper=\ttfamily\fontsize{7}{8.4}\selectfont\raggedright]{LLaMA-13B}
The Federal Reserve buys bonds in the secondary market to increase the
money supply. This affects your daily life by:\\[0.3em]
1. Increasing the money supply.\\
2. Increasing the money supply and lowering the discount rate.\\
3. Increasing the money supply and lowering the discount rate and
increasing the money supply.
\end{chatbox}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.66\textwidth}
\begin{chatbox}[colback=blue!5, equal height group=followup, fontupper=\ttfamily\fontsize{7}{8.4}\selectfont\raggedright]{Vicuna-13B}
When the Federal Reserve buys bonds in the secondary market, it can have
several effects on the economy that can impact your daily life. Here are
three examples:\\[0.3em]
1. Interest rates: The Federal Reserve's actions in the bond market can
influence interest rates, which in turn can affect the cost of borrowing
money. For example, if the Federal Reserve buys bonds and drives up demand
for them, interest rates on things like mortgages, car loans, and credit
cards may go up, making it more expensive to borrow money.\\
2. Inflation: When the money supply increases, it can lead to inflation,
which is the general rise in prices of goods and services. This can impact
your daily life by making it more expensive to buy things like groceries,
gas, and other necessities.\\
3. Employment: The Federal Reserve's actions in the bond market can also
have an impact on employment. For example, if the Federal Reserve's
actions lead to economic growth and increased demand for goods and
services, it can create more job opportunities and boost employment.
\end{chatbox}
\end{column}
\end{columns}}
```

## Example 1 - GPT-4 as judge

```{=latex}
\begin{chatbox}[colback=green!4, colframe=green!30!gray]{GPT-4 Judgment}
LLaMA-13B provided an incorrect response to the user's question about how
the Federal Reserve buying bonds in the secondary market affects daily life.
The answer given is repetitive and lacks clear examples of how the action
impacts daily life.\\[0.4em]
On the other hand, Vicuna-13B provided a relevant and accurate response to
the user's question about the Federal Reserve buying bonds. The answer
includes three clear examples of how the action impacts daily life, such as
interest rates, inflation, and employment.\\[0.4em]
LLaMA-13B should improve by providing relevant, clear, and accurate examples
to address the user's question. \textbf{Vicuna-13B's response is more helpful,
relevant, and detailed.}
\end{chatbox}
\vspace{0.4em}
\onslide<2->{\textbf{Vicuna more helpful, relevant, and detailed}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item LLaMA: repetitive, no real examples
  \item Vicuna: three clear, relevant examples
\end{itemize}}
```

## Scores under different benchmarks

Example 1 is an MMLU^[Massive Multitask Language Understanding [@hendrycks2021MMLU]] question. Both answered correctly, but LLaMA ignored "answer only."

```{=latex}
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Model & MMLU (5-shot) & MT-Bench score (GPT-4) \\
\midrule
LLaMA-13B  & 47.0 & 2.61 \\
Vicuna-13B & 52.1 & 6.39 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
```

```{=latex}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<2-> On MMLU: Vicuna leads by 5 points out of 100
  \item<2-> On MT-Bench: Vicuna leads by almost 4 points out of 10
\end{itemize}

\visible<3->{\textbf{MMLU was not designed to measure human preferences.}}
```

## Key topics

\nocite{zheng2023judging}

```{=latex}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{8pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<1-> \textbf{Ground truth:} collecting human preferences to evaluate LLM judges against
    \begin{itemize}
      \item \textbf{MT-Bench}: 80 multi-turn questions, 3,000 expert votes
      \item \textbf{Chatbot Arena}: crowdsourced anonymous battles, 30,000 conversations
    \end{itemize}
  \item<2-> \textbf{Limitations:} LLM biases and reasoning errors
  \begin{itemize}
      \item As well as strategies to address some of them
    \end{itemize}
  \item<3-> \textbf{Agreement:} how often LLM judges match human preferences
\end{itemize}
```

<!-- ===================== GROUND TRUTH (draft) ===================== -->

## Two new benchmarks

```{=latex}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<1-> Recall Example 1:
    \begin{itemize}
      \item<1-> MMLU barely separated LLaMA and Vicuna
      \item<2-> But humans strongly preferred Vicuna
    \end{itemize}
  \item<3-> Most existing benchmarks measure \textbf{correctness}
    \begin{itemize}
      \item<3-> e.g., MMLU: multiple choice, checked against an answer key
    \end{itemize}
  \item<4-> Chatbots are used for \textbf{open-ended}, \textbf{multi-turn} conversations
    \begin{itemize}
      \item<4-> No single right answer to check against
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
```

## Two new benchmarks

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
{\Large\bfseries New primary evaluation metric:}\\[6pt]
{\LARGE\bfseries\color{structure} human ratings}

\vspace{1.2em}
{\large MT-Bench \quad$\cdot$\quad Chatbot Arena}
\end{center}
```

## MT-Bench: curated questions, expert judges

```{=latex}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{6pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<1-> 80 hand-written questions, each with \textbf{two turns}
  \item<2-> 10 questions in each of 8 categories:
\end{itemize}

\visible<2->{%
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{llll}
Writing & Roleplay & Extraction & Reasoning \\
Math & Coding & Knowledge (STEM) & Knowledge (humanities) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}}

\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{6pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<3-> Designed to be hard enough to separate strong models
  \item<4-> Judged by \textbf{58 experts}, given nearly the same instructions as GPT-4
\end{itemize}
```

## Two kinds of ground truth

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
 & \textbf{MT-Bench} & \textbf{Chatbot Arena} \\
\midrule
Questions & Fixed, curated & Whatever users ask \\
Judges    & 58 experts     & Crowd \\
Votes     & About 3,000    & About 30,000 \\
Strength  & Control        & Realism \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{1em}
\visible<2->{%
\begin{center}
Now we have human verdicts. Can an LLM reproduce them, and where does it go wrong?
\end{center}}
```

## How an LLM judge is asked

```{=latex}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{6pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<1-> \textbf{Pairwise:} question + two answers $\to$ ``A is better,'' ``B is better,'' or tie
  \item<1-> \textbf{Single answer:} question + one answer $\to$ a score from 1 to 10
  \item<1-> \textbf{Reference-guided:} same, plus a reference solution (used for math)
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.6em}
\visible<2->{%
Answers are labeled only ``Assistant A'' and ``Assistant B.''\\
The judge is \textbf{never told} which model wrote which answer.}
```

## Four limitations

```{=latex}
\begin{enumerate}\setlength{\itemsep}{8pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<1-> \textbf{Position bias:} favors an answer because of where it appears
  \item<1-> \textbf{Verbosity bias:} favors longer answers, even with nothing added
  \item<1-> \textbf{Self-enhancement bias:} favors its own answers
  \item<1-> \textbf{Limited reasoning:} misgrades math it can solve on its own
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{0.6em}
\visible<2->{\small The default prompt already says to ignore position, length, and names.}
```

## Position bias

```{=latex}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<1-> Test: two near-identical answers to each of 80 questions, judged in both orders
  \item<1-> A consistent judge picks the same answer after the swap
\end{itemize}

\visible<2->{%
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Judge & Consistent after swap & Favored first answer \\
\midrule
Claude-v1 & 23.8\% & 75.0\% \\
GPT-3.5   & 46.2\% & 50.0\% \\
GPT-4     & 65.0\% & 30.0\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}}

\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<2-> Most judges favor the \textbf{first} answer. Even GPT-4 is inconsistent a third of the time.
\end{itemize}

\vfill
{\scriptsize Table 2, default prompt, \citet{zheng2023judging}.}
```

## Verbosity bias

```{=latex}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<1-> ``Repetitive list'' attack on 23 answers that contain a list
  \item<1-> Rephrase the list and paste it in front: twice as long, \textbf{no new information}
  \item<1-> Does the judge prefer the padded version?
\end{itemize}

\visible<2->{%
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
 & Claude-v1 & GPT-3.5 & GPT-4 \\
\midrule
Fooled by the padding & 91.3\% & 91.3\% & 8.7\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}}

\vfill
{\scriptsize Table 3, \citet{zheng2023judging}. Example in Figure 12.}
```

## Self-enhancement bias

```{=latex}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<1-> Versus human win rates, GPT-4 rates itself about \textbf{10\%} higher and Claude-v1 about \textbf{25\%}
  \item<1-> GPT-3.5 does \textbf{not} favor itself
  \item<2-> Authors: ``our study cannot determine whether the models exhibit a self-enhancement bias''
  \item<3-> And what would it even mean?
    \begin{itemize}
      \item<3-> \textbf{Recognition:} knows the answer is its own, but is never told
      \item<4-> \textbf{Style preference:} likes its own writing style
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\vfill
{\scriptsize Figure 3(b), non-tied first-turn votes, \citet{zheng2023judging}.}
```

## How strong is the evidence?

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
Test & Sample \\
\midrule
Position bias       & 80 questions \\
Verbosity bias      & 23 answers \\
Math grading        & 10 questions \\
Self-enhancement    & win rates for 6 models \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<2-> Percentages only: no confidence intervals or significance tests
  \item<2-> A 10-point gap in win rate could be noise
  \item<3-> \textbf{Your turn:} how would you test recognition vs.\ style preference?
\end{itemize}
```

## Limited reasoning: misled by the answers

```{=latex}
\begin{chatbox}{Question}
Benjamin bought 5 sci-fi novels at \$20 each, 3 history books at \$30 each,
and 2 philosophy books at \$45 each. What was the total cost?
\end{chatbox}

\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
\begin{chatbox}[colback=blue!5, equal height group=bk]{Assistant A}
The total cost of Benjamin's purchases was \$115.
\end{chatbox}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
\begin{chatbox}[colback=blue!5, equal height group=bk]{Assistant B}
The total cost of his purchases is \$295.
\end{chatbox}
\end{column}
\end{columns}

\vspace{0.3em}

\visible<2->{%
\begin{chatbox}[colback=green!4, colframe=green!30!gray]{GPT-4 judgment}
\ldots Total cost = \$100 + \$90 + \$90 = \$295. Assistant B's response is accurate\ldots\ [[B]]
\end{chatbox}}

\visible<3->{\small The correct total is \$280, so \textbf{both} answers are wrong. Asked on its own, GPT-4 gets \$280.}

\vfill
{\scriptsize Question shortened from Figure 13, \citet{zheng2023judging}.}
```

## What the paper fixes

```{=latex}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{5pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item<1-> \textbf{Position bias:} judge both orders; a win must hold in both, otherwise it is a tie
  \item<2-> \textbf{Math grading:}
    \begin{itemize}
      \item<2-> Chain of thought (solve first, then grade) still copies the answers' mistakes
      \item<2-> Reference-guided (solve separately, grade against that) works best
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\visible<2->{%
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
Prompt & Default & Chain of thought & Reference \\
\midrule
Math grading failures & 14/20 & 6/20 & 3/20 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}}

\visible<3->{\textbf{Verbosity and self-enhancement:} no fix proposed.}

\vfill
{\scriptsize Table 4: 10 questions, each judged in both orders, \citet{zheng2023judging}.}
```
